chapter_theme: The Vidyadhara wedding: the groom and bride are bathed, the priest lays the hall and tends the fire, the bride is given and led round the fire, the priests are paid and the onlookers go away amazed or to the forest.

cast.role: the kings who gather at the wedding, with their elephants
the women who ride in to the wedding on cow-elephants
the youth who weds; named by epithets and unnamed in these verses
the bride, the Vidyadhara king's daughter; unnamed in these verses
the Vidyadharas who bring holy waters for the bride's bath
the people who watch the wedding
the sacred-thread priest who prepares and tends the wedding fire
the hill-king, the bride's father, who gives her to the groom
the kin of the bride and groom who give wealth to the priests

1085.reading: Kings with lotus-bright faces gather in numbers, riding war elephants whose fly-whisks and flower-wreathed foreheads are splashed by the waves of water thrown over them.
1085.event: Kings come to the wedding in crowds on their elephants.

1086.reading: Women with rain-cloud eyes and flower garlands crowd every direction on their cow-elephants, leaving no room, and look like dark peacocks spread over those who see them.
1086.event: Women ride in to the wedding and fill the roads.

1087.reading: The lord sits on a gem seat under the lion-throne in front of the jewelled mansions, with warrior kings around him, like the full moon among stars.
1087.nuance: The word காளை, the youth, is taken to name the groom as in the earlier chapters; the verse does not name him.
1087.event: The groom sits enthroned among kings before the wedding bath.

1088.reading: The youth bathes as auspicious pots are lifted and the water poured over him, and looks like a great mountain over which rain-clouds have emptied.
1088.nuance: The word division is broken in line 1 and the edition's தம் உடன் reading is held loosely.
1088.event: Pots of water are poured over the groom in the wedding bath.

1089.reading: After the kings' pouring of jewelled water and a rain of flowers from the sky, the youth puts on gold ornaments and enters the new city of the sacrifice.
1089.event: The groom finishes his bath, dresses and enters the wedding city.

1090.reading: The Vidyadharas come down from the heights with water from the Ganga and other streams for the bride's bath, so thickly that the sky has no room, and the poet asks what more need be said.
1090.event: Vidyadharas descend with holy waters for the bride's bath.

1091.reading: Water from the six great mountains' streams bathes the delicate bride, and then a rain of flowers of every kind is made to fall on her.
1091.event: The bride is bathed with mountain water and flowers.

1092.reading: A sandal rain pours and a wind carries drops of honey, so that the people are bewildered whether this is a king's world or another age and some are amazed and some glad.
1092.event: Sandal-rain and a scented breeze fall as the bride is dressed.

1093.reading: Dressed in the gifts of the sky-dwellers and praised with songs, the red-eyed bride reaches the sacrifice city.
1093.nuance: Her title is only நங்கை and the red-eyed one, as elsewhere in this chapter; the verse never names her.
1093.event: The bride, adorned, comes to the wedding hall.

1094.reading: Before the bride arrives, the sacred-thread priest adorns the wedding hall and the rest arrange to tend the fire there.
1094.event: The priest and the others prepare the hall and the fire before the bride arrives.

1095.reading: The priest has the gem floor smeared with sandal and wax, marks it with a golden rod, has it smeared again with fragrance, and learns its measure by reciting the Veda.
1095.nuance: The edition's வுலகு/அதனாரிடம் word division is broken in line 4, so the reading of ஆரிடம் is held loosely.
1095.event: The priest prepares and marks the ground for the fire.

claims.claim: the ground of the rite must be prepared and its measure learned by reciting the Veda

1096.reading: He lays out a square of pearl-sand, ringed with raised ground, and spreads darbha grass on it with the tips toward the north and east, and performs a rite over it.
1096.event: The priest lays out the square of sand and spreads darbha.

claims.claim: the sacred grass is laid with its tips to the north and east for the rite

1097.reading: The priest sets guards for the four-faced one's right and the quarters, spreads the sacrificial sticks and, in the due order, sits to recite and tend them.
1097.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard; the lines about the four-faced Brahma's right side may belong to the rite's layout and the sense is not fixed.
1097.event: The priest sets the sacrificial sticks and begins the fire-rite.

1098.reading: The lord of the gods, the minister of the asuras and the moon are said to enter the sky, and the astrologer declares that this is the hour with the garland of the ocean.
1098.nuance: Line 1 names நடுக்கடலுளான், the one in mid-ocean, and அமரராசான், but the identity of each figure and the speaker are only inferred from context.

1099.reading: Before the fire the hill-king gives the bride to the groom with water, and the lotus-born lady comes with her.
1099.event: The bride's father gives her to the groom, pouring water, before the fire.

claims.claim: the fire raised for the rite stands as the god before whom the bride is given

1100.reading: With kusa grass braided and held at his right side, the spear-bearing youth sits before the fire beside the maiden, like the radiant moon beside the maid.
1100.event: The groom sits beside the bride at the fire.

1101.reading: Smoke from the fire rises like a dark cloud as the priest tends it and offers into the flame, while the youth in his own mind offers himself to the girl.
1101.nuance: The verse pairs the priest's burning offering with the groom's desire; the same word வேட்டான் is used of both, once for the sacrifice and once for the wish.
1101.event: The priest feeds the sacrificial fire as the groom longs for the bride.

1102.reading: Once the fire-rite has been honoured, the youth rises, takes the soft fingers of the girl and walks with her on his right, like the dark sea joined with the Ganga.
1102.event: The groom takes the bride's hand and walks around the fire.

1103.reading: As the hero takes her flower-hand she trembles with hair on end and sweat on her brow and cannot set her red feet down, and the poet asks who can tell the shyness of the peacock-like girl.
1103.event: The bride shakes and perspires as the groom clasps her hand.

1104.reading: More rites go by and many things are said, and the kin of the girl and of the youth, mingled together, pour out heaps of gold and gems to the priests who keep the fire.
1104.event: The two families give gold and gems to the fire-priests.

1105.reading: The chief priest, skilled in the six limbs, four Vedas and countless ritual books, is made to receive a rain of wealth like the conch treasure.
1105.event: The expert priest is given a rain of wealth.

claims.claim: the priest learned in the limbs, the four Vedas and the kalpa deserves the gift of wealth

1106.reading: One shows the peacock-like bride the Vadameen star shining in the sky, and she scorns herself, asking whether she, shameless and lowly, can look at the world as that star does.
1106.nuance: The speaker is taken to be the bride from இகழ்ந்தாள், and the meaning of the self-reproach is not settled; the star is Arundhati only by the ritual's usual order, not by the verse's word.
1106.event: The bride is shown the star and reproaches herself.

1107.reading: As the wedding rites go on, some who see such wealth go off to the forest to practise great penance, and others, wondering whether it ever comes even in a dream, turn back.
1107.nuance: The verse stops at the departures and does not say that the penance is a judgment on the wedding; the 'dream' phrase is a spoken wonder, not a doctrinal claim.
1107.event: Onlookers either leave for the forest to do penance or turn home amazed.

claims.claim: the wealth of the wedding is so great that it may be taken for a dream and so is to be left for the forest penance

links.note: Naladiyar 23 sees wedding drums that may be funeral drums by evening; Soolamani 1107 ends the rites with some who leave for the forest and some who go home amazed at the wealth.
links.teaches: The same festival shows the transience of the day for some and wonder for others, so the Soolamani lets the Naladiyar's lesson be heard only by those who leave.

gains.a: The wedding verse gains a rule of why some depart to the forest, which the verse leaves unsaid.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a scene where its lesson is taken by some and missed by others, which it states only as a rule for the wise.

links.note: 1040 has the bride praying to the Jina to lose the disease of birth; 1107 ends her wedding with some going to the forest and others returning to enjoy.
links.teaches: The wedding that the maiden began by praying to be freed of birth closes on the same two answers, release or return.

links.note: 1101 shows the priest's fire fed while the groom's desire is kindled; Siddhar 147 asks when he will kindle the homa fire inside to cross the sea of desire.
links.teaches: One fire serves desire on one side and ends desire on the other, so the rite is the same fire put to opposite uses.

gains.a: The wedding fire gains a rival use, as a fire inside the body that ends the desire it kindles in the groom.
gains.b: The Siddhar's inner homa gains the outward rite it turns inward, with a priest's actual oblation set beside the longing.

links.note: Kural 1011 says true shame is shame at wrongdoing and anything else is only the shame of women; 1103 gives the bride's trembling shyness at the first clasp.
links.teaches: The bride's shyness is the kind the Kural calls a woman's own and not yet the shame of deeds, so the verse shows what the couplet sets aside.

gains.a: The bride's trembling gains a name for what it is, the shame of the bright-browed that the Kural separates from moral shame.
gains.b: The couplet gains a living case of the shame it sets aside, which it names without showing.

links.note: 1099 has the hill-king give the bride with water before the fire as god; Naladiyar 56 says marriage is called கடி because it binds the husband even to a faulty wife.
links.teaches: The giving of the bride before the fire is the act that creates the hardship of binding which Naladiyar names, so the rite explains why the husband cannot put her away.

gains.a: The gift before the fire gains a consequence, the lasting duty it puts on the groom.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the actual rite of water and fire that makes the binding.

links.note: 1103 shows the bride's shyness at the hand-clasp; 1106 has her scorn herself as shameless when shown the star.
links.teaches: Her shyness grows from trembling in the body to a spoken reproach, so the poet follows one feeling across the rite.

links.note: 1088 bathes the groom with water poured from pots; 1091 bathes the bride with mountain water and flowers.
links.teaches: Both are bathed before the fire but she is bathed by the Vidyadharas from above and he by kings, so the two sides bring different guests.

links.note: 1099 has the father give the bride with water; 1102 has the groom lead her round the fire holding her fingers.
links.teaches: The gift only becomes a marriage when the groom takes her hand and walks the fire, so the two verses give the two halves of the one act.

links.note: 1104 has both families pour gold and gems on the priests; 1105 names the learned chief priest who gets the greatest rain of wealth.
links.teaches: The gift is shared out by the priest's learning, so the wealth follows the Veda and not the families.

source_issues: Verses 1085 to 1107 have broken word division in many lines (for example the splits in 1089, 1095 and 1098).
Verse 1098: the figures named in lines 1 and 2 and the speaker of line 4 are doubtful.
Verse 1106: the speaker and the star's name are inferred from context.
